scenes.title: Spot Options vs. Futures Options Put-Call Parity

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Observability: Fischer Black's model utilizes directly observable futures prices F0, bypassing spot storage cost and convenience yield errors ([fact-07]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Parity Equation: c + K*e^(-r*T) = p + F0*e^(-r*T) discounts both strike K and futures price F0 to present value ([fact-03]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Break down Zero-Drift Assumption: futures contracts cost nothing to enter, treating q = r as a continuous dividend yield ([fact-04]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Break down Black's Formula: c = e^(-r*T) * [F0 * N(d1) - K * N(d2)] incorporating standardized variables d1 and d2 ([fact-05]).

scenes.title: Spot Calls vs. American Futures Calls Early Exercise

beatOutlines.textOutline: Balance Spot Calls: non-dividend spot calls are rarely exercised early because exercising forfeits time value ([fact-09]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Balance Futures Calls: American futures calls are exercised early when F is high, expected to decline, or interest rates are high to earn interest on cash F - K ([fact-09]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

scenes.title: Terminal Gross Payoff vs. Compounded Net Trading Profit

beatOutlines.textOutline: Plot Terminal Gross Payoff: max(F_T - K, 0) at option expiration for futures call contracts ([fact-11]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Plot Net Trading Profit: Payoff minus initial premium paid compounded at risk-free rate (Payoff - Premium * e^(r*T)) ([fact-11]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

scenes.title: Binomial Tree Parameterization for Futures Options

beatOutlines.textOutline: Up and Down Factors: u = e^(sigma * sqrt(delta_t)) and d = 1 / u matching volatility sigma ([fact-08]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Risk-Neutral Probability: p = (1 - d) / (u - d), replacing drift e^(r*delta_t) with 1 due to zero initial payment for futures ([fact-08]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

summarySteps: 1. Futures Option Exercise ([fact-01]): Exercising a call delivers a long futures position plus cash F0 - K; exercising a put delivers short futures plus K - F0.
2. Trader Preferences ([fact-02]): Futures options are preferred over spot options due to superior liquidity, no physical delivery friction, and seamless margin netting.
3. Put-Call Parity ([fact-03]): c + K*e^(-r*T) = p + F0*e^(-r*T) discounts both futures price F0 and strike K to present value.
4. Zero-Drift Assumption ([fact-04]): Futures contracts cost nothing to enter, behaving in risk-neutral valuation like assets paying continuous dividend q = r.
5. Fischer Black's Model ([fact-05]): Values futures options using F0 in place of S0: c = e^(-r*T) * [F0 * N(d1) - K * N(d2)].
6. Observable Inputs ([fact-07]): Financial institutions prefer Black's model because F0 is directly observable, bypassing spot storage cost and convenience yield errors.
7. Binomial Tree Probability ([fact-08]): Futures binomial lattices use modified up probability p = (1 - d) / (u - d) with drift replaced by 1.
8. American Early Exercise ([fact-09]): American futures calls are optimally exercised early when futures prices are high, expected to decline, or interest rates are high.
bottomTakeaway: Fischer Black's (1976) model prices futures options by treating futures contracts as zero-drift assets (q = r), providing institutional traders with observable valuation inputs and flexible cash-settled exercise mechanics ([fact-01], [fact-04], [fact-05], [fact-07]).
